articles.author: Payout Rail
articles.description:
ACH Return Codes Demystified: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Each
When an ACH payment fails, the originating financial institution receives a return code. Understanding what each code means—and how to respond—is critical for any developer building payment infrastructure. Unlike generic error messages, ACH return codes follow the NACHA (National Automated Clearing House Association) standard and map to specific, actionable failure reasons.
ACH transfers are not instantaneous. A payout initiated today may settle in 1–2 business days, and returns can arrive days or even weeks later. If your system doesn't decode and act on return codes, you'll miss critical signals: Is the account closed? Did the customer dispute the charge? Is there insufficient funding? Each scenario demands a different respo…
articles.title: ACH Return Codes Demystified: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Each

articles.author: SamFware
articles.description:
Open Odin and the Options tab looks like a row of checkboxes nobody dares to touch. Most guides say "leave everything at default" and move on, which is fine until something goes wrong and you need to know what the checkbox you just ticked actually did. Here's what the important ones do, in plain terms.
Auto Reboot. The default. After the flash completes, Odin tells the phone to reboot into the freshly written system. You want this on for a normal flash. The only time people turn it off is when they're chaining operations — for example, flashing firmware and then immediately booting into recovery to wipe cache — because an automatic reboot would skip the window where you can catch the recovery key combo. For a standard flash, leave it on.
F. Reset Time. Also on by default, and also somethin…

articles.description:
An AI general ledger works when the model only produces proposals (a category, a match, a question with a confidence) and deterministic code validates, applies, logs and can reverse them. Every balance and total comes from the ledger, never the model. That is how ZeraBooks is built. This post sketches that shape in TypeScript. It illustrates the design; it isn't our source code.
I'm on the ZeraBooks team. When people hear "AI does the bookkeeping" they picture a model writing journal entries. That's the design we avoided. The model never writes to the ledger and never does arithmetic. It returns a small structured proposal, and everything after that is ordinary code with tests.

To disable Rovo in Jira, an organization admin adds Jira to the blocklist on the Rovo access page in Atlassian Administration. We did exactly that on our own test org on 22 October 2026, and two minutes later five AI entry points had gone from Jira. Five others were still there, though. And when we asked Rovo Chat to summarise a Jira work item, with Jira still on the blocklist, it summarised it correctly, three times over half an hour.
So "disable" means less than most admins hope. The block turns off the AI features that belong to Jira itself. articles.description:
The failure is always the same shape. The visitor presses submit, PHP makes one wp_remote_post() call, the CRM answers 502 or the connection hangs until the request is killed, and the lead exists nowhere. The visitor saw a thank-you message. Nobody follows up.
This is the version I would ship: write the lead into a queue table inside WordPress first, then let a worker deliver it with backoff, an idempotency key, and a dead-letter state that a human is forced to look at. Everything below is one must-use plugin.
The outbound request blocks the visitor. The default timeout is generous, the form looks frozen, and people press submit again.
A retryable error is treated as success. 429, 500, 502, 503 and connection timeouts are the normal case, not the exception.
A permanent error is invisible. …
